transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. I... well, I hope I'm not taking up too much of your time with this. It's probably just a silly little habit, really, but... I came because I seem to be spending a bit too much of my day checking on things. 

I just... I find myself opening the same folders, and my desk drawers, and these little labeled boxes I have, over and over. Just to make sure all my important papers and family keepsakes are right where I left them. And, um... sometimes I'll go back and look again even if I just checked them a few minutes before. 

I just like to be absolutely certain they're safe, you know? It sounds a bit foolish when I say it out loud... it's not too terribly unusual to want to be careful with important things, is it?
Do you find yourself having persistent, unwanted thoughts that something bad might happen if you don’t check these things repeatedly?

Oh, I wouldn't say I think something truly dreadful will happen... I certainly don't want to sound dramatic. But, well... yes, I suppose I do get these little thoughts. 

Even when I know better, a thought will just keep needling me. I'll start worrying that I might have accidentally thrown away my husband's old tax papers, or... or maybe I slipped a special family recipe into the wrong box. And I just can't seem to let the thought pass without feeling like I've done something terribly careless. I just have to go make sure I haven't made a mess of things. 

Does that make sense? I hope I'm explaining it properly for you. I know it sounds like such a fuss over nothing.
Do these thoughts cause you a lot of anxiety or distress, and does checking the items actually make you feel better, even if just for a short time?

Oh my, distress is a rather strong word, isn't it? I wouldn't want you to think I'm sitting at home in a panic or anything like that. I really try not to be a bother to anyone with it. It's... it's more of an uncomfortable little itch in my mind. Just a mild sort of worry, really. 

But yes, when I do go and check the folders, it certainly does make me feel better. It puts my mind right at ease just seeing everything exactly where it belongs. It's just... well, sometimes that settled feeling doesn't last quite as long as I'd like, and I feel the need to just peek one more time. 

I hope I'm answering your questions alright? I know you must deal with people who have real, serious problems, and here I am fussing over old receipts... I do hope I'm giving you the information you need.
How much time do you spend each day checking these things, and does it ever get in the way of doing other things you need or want to do?

Well... time... it's hard to say exactly, isn't it? Time just sort of slips away when you're busy tidying up. I suppose... well, it might be a bit more than just a few minutes here and there. 

I really try not to let it interfere with anything important, I promise you that. But, um... well, I have had to call off a few of my mentoring sessions with the young ladies at the church lately. And I missed my book club last week. It's just... I'll start checking the boxes after lunch, and before I know it, the whole afternoon has gone by. 

And then, well... I get so flustered, and sometimes I've pulled so many papers out to check them that the living room looks a bit untidy. I just couldn't bear to have anyone come over and see the apartment in such a state. It's terribly embarrassing, really. A woman my age ought to have her home in perfect order, shouldn't she? 

I do hope I'm not sounding like a complete recluse. I still keep busy, mostly. Is... is it normal to lose track of time like that when you're just trying to be organized?
Do you ever try to resist or stop the thoughts about needing to check your papers and boxes, or do you feel like the checking is something you have to do to feel right?

Oh, I certainly try to just brush them aside. I tell myself, 'Now, you know perfectly well everything is fine.' But... well, like I was trying to explain earlier, even when I absolutely know better, that little thought just keeps needling at me. 

I'll try to sit and read, but then the worry creeps in again that I might have accidentally tossed out my husband's old tax papers, or... or maybe put a special family recipe in the completely wrong box. I really do try to stop thinking about it, but I just can't seem to let it pass without feeling like I've done something terribly careless. So I suppose... yes, I do end up feeling like I just have to go look, just to prove to myself I haven't been irresponsible. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound too foolish? I know it's silly to fret over such small things, and I really do try my best to be sensible about it. I hope I'm answering exactly what you're asking?

Have you noticed that these thoughts ever take the form of vivid images or impulses that pop into your mind, rather than just being worries about things you might have actually done or might really do?

Oh, goodness no, I wouldn't say I have impulses or anything quite so dramatic as that. I don't want you to think I'm having strange visions or anything untoward. 

It's really just... well, just those little nagging worries I mentioned. Just a thought that maybe I've been a bit careless with my organizing. I don't see pictures in my head or feel like I'm going to do something out of the ordinary. It's all very mundane, really. Just an old woman fretting over her paperwork. 

I hope that's alright? I know you must see people with much more vivid imaginations than mine. Am I giving you the right sort of answers for your notes?
Would you say that the time you spend checking your papers and boxes adds up to more than an hour each day?

Well... oh dear. I suppose if you were to add it all up, it... it probably does amount to more than an hour. Maybe quite a bit more, if I'm being perfectly honest. I feel a bit foolish admitting it, but that's really why I finally decided to come see you. 

I just... I find myself spending far too much of my day opening the very same folders and drawers. And those labeled boxes I mentioned. I'll open them again and again, just to make absolutely sure the important papers and family keepsakes are exactly where I left them. Even when I know I just checked them a few minutes before! 

It sounds so silly when I say it out loud, doesn't it? I just want to be thorough and keep everything nice and orderly, but I know it's gotten a bit out of hand. I hope you don't think I'm completely losing my wits. Is that... is that the sort of thing you were asking about?
Do you feel that you have to perform these checking behaviors in a certain way or a specific number of times to feel reassured or to prevent something bad from happening?

Oh, heavens no. I don't have any sort of... well, any special rituals or magic numbers or anything like that. I don't want to give you the wrong impression. 

It's not as if I have to tap the box three times or... or count to ten before I open a folder. And I certainly don't think anything dreadful is going to happen, like a fire or a terrible accident, just because I didn't check. It's nothing quite so dramatic. 

I just... I just look until I feel certain I haven't been careless. Until I can tell myself, 'See, you put it in the right place, everything is fine.' It's just about being thorough, really. 

I do hope that makes sense? I wouldn't want you to think I was doing anything terribly bizarre. I'm just trying to be a responsible person, even if I go a bit overboard sometimes. Is that... does that answer your question alright?
Do you ever feel the need to arrange or rearrange your papers or items in a specific order or way, beyond just checking to make sure they’re there?

Oh, no... no, I don't think I do that. Once the papers are in their proper folders, I don't feel any need to... well, to line them up perfectly or organize them in a special pattern or anything like that. 

It's really just about making sure they haven't gone missing, just like we talked about. As long as they are safely in the box where they belong, I'm quite satisfied. I certainly don't sit there arranging them by size or color or anything fussy like that! 

I hope I'm not being difficult by saying no to that? I know you're asking these questions for a very good reason, and I do want to be as helpful as I can. I just wouldn't want to mislead you into thinking I have habits that I don't actually have. Am I still doing alright with my answers?
Are there any other things you feel you must do repeatedly, such as washing your hands, cleaning, or something else, that might be related to these worries?

Oh, goodness, no. Nothing like that. I don't... I don't wash my hands any more than a normal person would, just before meals or after using the washroom, of course. I like keeping a tidy house, but I certainly don't scrub the floors repeatedly or anything of that sort. 

My little... habit, I suppose you could call it, is really just confined to those papers and boxes we discussed. I don't have any other peculiar routines. I do try very hard to be sensible about everything else. 

I hope that's the right answer? I want to make sure I'm giving you all the information you need, but I truly don't have any of those other worries. I'm not being too troublesome, am I?

Have you ever had any other recurring thoughts, mental images, or urges that bother you and make you feel like you have to do something to reduce the discomfort, even if it's not related to checking your papers or boxes?

Oh, goodness me, no. I don't... I don't have any strange pictures popping into my head or... or sudden urges to do things. Nothing like that at all. Aside from that silly business with my papers, my mind is usually quite peaceful. I try to focus on pleasant things, you know, like my reading. 

I feel almost terrible saying no to so many of your questions! I do hope I'm not being a disappointing patient for you. You're being so thorough and kind, and I really don't want you to think I'm hiding anything from you. It truly is just the checking we talked about. 

Is it... is it alright that I don't have anything else to report? I just want to be sure I'm doing a good job answering your questions.
Has this checking habit affected your relationships with others, or caused you to avoid certain activities or situations because of embarrassment or the time it takes?

Well... I suppose it has, a little bit. I... I really don't like to admit this, because it sounds so dreadful, but... there have been times when I've had to cancel my mentoring sessions with the young ladies at the church. And... and my book club, too. 

It's just that sometimes, I... well, I lose whole afternoons to checking the papers, and before I know it, the time has just slipped away from me. And then my apartment is all in disarray from having the boxes out, and I... I just feel too embarrassed to have anyone over when it looks like that. It's so silly of me, I know. A woman my age should be able to keep a schedule. 

I do try my best to make up for it, though! I always send a nice note when I have to cancel. I hope... I hope you don't think too poorly of me for letting it get in the way of my commitments. I know it's not the proper way to behave. Am I... am I giving you the right sort of information? I want to make sure I'm doing this correctly for you.
When you feel that nagging worry about possibly having misplaced something important, does it feel like the only way to make that feeling go away is to actually check the papers and boxes?

Well, yes... I suppose that's exactly it. It's... it's just this silly little nagging feeling. I try so hard to just ignore it, to sit down with a cup of tea and my book, but... I just can't seem to settle until I've looked. 

I know it sounds so foolish. I mean, I know perfectly well I just checked the blue folder not five minutes ago, and the birth certificates were right there. But the worry just... it just sort of builds up inside me, and the only way to make it stop is to go back and open the folder, and the drawer, and the boxes again. Just to be absolutely certain. 

I spend... well, I spend rather a lot of my day doing it, I'm afraid. Far more than I should. That's really why I came to see you. I hope... I hope that makes sense? I know it's not very logical of me. Does that help explain it properly for you?

When you have these worries about possibly misplacing something, do they feel different from ordinary worries, like they are intrusive, unwanted, and come into your mind in a way that feels out of your control?

Well... I wouldn't want to use a strong phrase like "out of control." That makes me sound quite unhinged, and I promise you I'm keeping my wits about me as best I can! I don't want you to think I'm losing my faculties. 

But... I suppose they are a bit different from ordinary, everyday worries. It's more like... well, even when I know better, a thought will just keep needling me. Out of nowhere, I'll suddenly worry that I might have accidentally thrown away my husband's old tax papers, or... or perhaps I put a cherished family recipe in the wrong box. 

And once that thought arrives, I just can't seem to let it pass. If I try to ignore it, it just sits there, and I start feeling like I've done something terribly, terribly careless. It's very bothersome, but I really do try not to let it get the better of me. 

It's so embarrassing to admit that my mind gets stuck on these little things. I hope I'm not sounding too silly to you... does that answer your question properly, Doctor? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need.

A woman my age should be able to keep a schedule. 

I do try my best to make up for it, though! I always send a nice note when I have to cancel. I hope... I hope you don't think too poorly of me for letting it get in the way of my commitments. I know it's not the proper way to behave. Am I... am I giving you the right sort of information? I want to make sure I'm doing this correctly for you.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the checking behavior is driven by a need to prevent or reduce anxiety, which would support a diagnosis of OCD (F42.2) over other specified OCD-related disorders (F42.8).
doctor.question: When you feel that nagging worry about possibly having misplaced something important, does it feel like the only way to make that feeling go away is to actually check the papers and boxes?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: I came because I spend far too much of my day opening the same folders, drawers, and labeled boxes again and again to make sure the important papers and keepsakes are where I left them, even when I just checked a few minutes before.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if checking the papers and boxes (the repetitive behavior) is performed in response to the nagging worry (the obsession) to make the feeling go away, which directly maps to the definition of compulsions.

patient.answer:
Well, yes... I suppose that's exactly it. It's... it's just this silly little nagging feeling. I try so hard to just ignore it, to sit down with a cup of tea and my book, but... I just can't seem to settle until I've looked. 

I know it sounds so foolish. I mean, I know perfectly well I just checked the blue folder not five minutes ago, and the birth certificates were right there. But the worry just... it just sort of builds up inside me, and the only way to make it stop is to go back and open the folder, and the drawer, and the boxes again. Just to be absolutely certain. 

I spend... well, I spend rather a lot of my day doing it, I'm afraid. Far more than I should. That's really why I came to see you. I hope... I hope that makes sense? I know it's not very logical of me. Does that help explain it properly for you?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences intrusive, obsessive thoughts that are not just worries about real-life problems, which would help distinguish between F42.2 (Mixed obsessional thoughts and acts) and F42.8 (Other specified obsessive-compulsive disorders).
doctor.question: When you have these worries about possibly misplacing something, do they feel different from ordinary worries, like they are intrusive, unwanted, and come into your mind in a way that feels out of your control?

target_item.name: Obsessions
target_item.manifestation: Even when I know better, a thought will keep needling me that I may have thrown away my husband's old tax papers or put a family recipe in the wrong box, and I can't seem to let it pass without feeling I've done something terribly careless.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the worries about misplacing things feel intrusive, unwanted, and out of control, which perfectly aligns with the definition of obsessions (S065).

patient.answer:
Well... I wouldn't want to use a strong phrase like "out of control." That makes me sound quite unhinged, and I promise you I'm keeping my wits about me as best I can! I don't want you to think I'm losing my faculties. 

But... I suppose they are a bit different from ordinary, everyday worries. It's more like... well, even when I know better, a thought will just keep needling me. Out of nowhere, I'll suddenly worry that I might have accidentally thrown away my husband's old tax papers, or... or perhaps I put a cherished family recipe in the wrong box. 

And once that thought arrives, I just can't seem to let it pass. If I try to ignore it, it just sits there, and I start feeling like I've done something terribly, terribly careless. It's very bothersome, but I really do try not to let it get the better of me. 

It's so embarrassing to admit that my mind gets stuck on these little things. I hope I'm not sounding too silly to you... does that answer your question properly, Doctor? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent intrusive thoughts related to potential misplacement of important documents, accompanied by repetitive checking behaviors aimed at reducing distress. These symptoms are consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder with predominantly checking behavior. There is no evidence of other OCD subtypes or comorbid conditions that would suggest other specified OCD-related disorders.
